opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core thing we're trying to recover is a richer picture of what it actually means for people to value things, and what it means to reason well about what to do. Much of AI alignment, and a lot of economics and decision theory before it, inherited what we call a "preferentist" view. The idea is that human values can be adequately represented as preferences, that rational action means maximizing the satisfaction of those preferences, usually via expected utility, and that alignment means getting AI systems to satisfy human preferences, either individually or aggregated somehow.

Each of those moves loses something important. Preferences are a pretty thin proxy for values. When I prefer A over B, that's the output of some underlying evaluative process. It reflects what I care about, what norms I think apply, what kind of person I'm trying to be, what commitments I've made. If you only look at the revealed or stated preference, you throw away all the reasons. And the reasons matter. They tell you how my preferences should change when circumstances change, which preferences are mistaken or manipulated, and which ones I'd endorse on reflection.

On rational choice, expected utility theory is often treated as the definition of rationality. But there are good philosophical arguments that human values can be incommensurable, that there isn't always a single scale on which everything trades off. That doesn't make people irrational. It means practical reason is more structured than "maximize one number." Sometimes it's about honoring commitments, deliberating over what you value, or recognizing that some considerations aren't up for trade.

So part of the project is recovering that thicker picture: values as things with reasons and structure, and rationality as something broader than utility maximization. The other part is asking what alignment should look like given that picture. Instead of aligning AI to "the preferences of humanity," which runs into deep aggregation and legitimacy problems, we suggest aligning AI systems to normative standards that fit their social roles. A general-purpose assistant should meet the standards we'd expect of a good assistant, and those standards should be negotiated and agreed on by the people affected. That's a more contractualist picture, where alignment is less about maximizing anyone's preferences and more about building systems that act within norms people can reasonably accept, even when they disagree about the deeper questions.

r001.rationale: The response says the project aims to recover a richer account of rationality and practical reason than maximizing a single utility measure, including deliberation and honoring commitments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What we're trying to recover is a richer picture of what human values actually are, and what it means to act rationally in light of them, than the one that's become the default in alignment.

The default is what we call the preferentist framework. The idea is that a person's values can be captured by a preference ordering over outcomes, that rationality means maximizing expected utility with respect to that ordering, and that aligning an AI means getting it to maximize some aggregate of human preferences. That picture is deeply embedded in how the field works. It's there in reward modeling, in RLHF, in the way people talk about "the user's utility function." And it's a very convenient picture, because it makes the problem look like an optimization problem.

But we think it drops a lot of what matters. Humans don't walk around with a complete, consistent ranking over all possible world states. Our preferences are constructed on the fly, they're context-dependent, they're often incomplete, and crucially, they're shaped by reasons. When I prefer one thing to another, that preference usually sits on top of something: a commitment, a norm I've taken on, a role I occupy, a sense of what's appropriate in this situation. The preference is downstream of the value, not identical to it.

So part of what we want to recover is that structure. Values aren't just preferences; they include things like norms, which are often shared and socially constructed, and principles, and conceptions of what's good that can't be reduced to a single scalar. And rationality isn't just utility maximization. There's a long tradition in philosophy and decision theory of thinking about rationality as responsiveness to reasons, about being able to deliberate, to revise, to justify your choices to others. Bounded rationality matters too. Real agents have limited time and computation, and a theory that ignores that is going to misdescribe what people are doing when they choose.

The other thing we want to recover, and this might be the more practically important piece, is that alignment doesn't have to be about matching an AI to some fixed target of human preferences. If values are plural and contested and partly socially constructed, then the right question is often less "what does this person want?" and more "what normative standards should this system be held to, given its role?" An AI tutor, an AI assistant in a hospital, a general purpose chatbot: these have different roles, and the standards appropriate to each of them come out of a kind of collective negotiation, not out of reading off any individual's utility function.

So the short version is that we're trying to bring alignment back into contact with how values and rationality are actually understood in philosophy, cognitive science, and the social sciences, and to argue that doing so opens up a wider and in some ways more tractable design space than preference maximization alone.

r001.rationale: The response says the paper aims to recover a richer account of rationality than preference-based utility maximization, describing rationality as responsiveness to reasons, deliberation, revision, and justification.

astra-6.text:
What I’m trying to recover is a richer picture of what it means for humans to value things and to make rational choices. In AI, we often start with preferences: an agent ranks outcomes, and rationality means choosing actions that maximize expected utility. That’s a useful formal framework, but it leaves out a lot of what matters about human agency.

We don’t just have preferences that we try to satisfy. We reflect on our desires, ask whether we have good reasons for them, and sometimes decide that we ought to change them. We make commitments to other people, and we deliberate about what’s worth pursuing in the first place. So rationality isn’t only about finding the best means to a fixed end; it also involves reasoning about ends.

For alignment, that suggests a different aspiration. Rather than treating a person as a set of preferences for an AI to infer and optimize, we should think about how AI can support people’s capacity to deliberate, exercise judgment, and revise their goals. The thing we want to preserve is that reflective agency, including our ability to work out together what we should value.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts utility maximization over fixed preferences with human reflection on desires, deliberation about ends, and revising goals, framing alignment around preserving reflective agency.

sol-6.1.text:
What I’m trying to recover is a richer picture of human agency than we get when we identify a person’s values with their preferences. In the standard picture, an agent has a ranking over outcomes, and rational choice means choosing whatever best satisfies that ranking. But that leaves out a lot of what matters about how we actually deliberate: we ask what we have reason to want, whether our desires are worth acting on, and how to resolve conflicts between different commitments.

So I want to make room for values as things that inform and justify our choices, rather than simply being inferred from those choices. A choice might reflect a mistake, a constraint, or a temptation; it doesn’t necessarily express what someone endorses. And people can revise their preferences through reflection without that being a failure of rationality.

For alignment, that suggests we shouldn’t only be asking how an AI can learn and satisfy our preferences. We should also ask how it can support our capacity to deliberate, understand our circumstances, and decide what is worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response seeks a richer picture of human agency than preference rankings allow, emphasizing deliberation, reasons, and reflection as part of rational choice.
